sources.title: Authentication & Session Design
sources.author: @alex_dev
sources.rawContent: Authentication uses stateless RS256 JWT tokens with 24h expiry. Tokens carry the role claim and are verified by a shared public key pinned in each service. We chose stateless tokens to keep the auth service simple. There is an open question about whether we need server-side revocation for admin-level tokens; the current design accepts that risk because revocation was out of scope for Q1.

facts.title: Session auth uses stateless RS256 JWT
facts.summary: Authentication uses stateless RS256 JWT tokens with a 24h expiry; revocation is out of scope.
facts.verbatimQuote: Authentication uses stateless RS256 JWT tokens with 24h expiry.

facts.title: No server-side token revocation
facts.summary: Stateless JWTs cannot be revoked; admin tokens carry that risk until a session store is introduced.
facts.verbatimQuote: There is an open question about whether we need server-side revocation for admin-level tokens; the current design accepts that risk because revocation was out of scope for Q1.

sources.title: feat: replace JWT middleware with ioredis sliding sessions
sources.author: @alex_dev
sources.rawContent: Replaced stateless JWT middleware with ioredis sliding session store (TTL 3600s) because stateless tokens could not be revoked during the May 2 rate-limit incident. The middleware now checks the session store on every authenticated request. The PR also adds a session revocation endpoint for admins. Deployed to production on May 5.

facts.title: Session store migration to ioredis sliding sessions
facts.summary: Auth was migrated from stateless JWTs to an ioredis sliding session store with a 3600s TTL and admin revocation support.
facts.verbatimQuote: Replaced stateless JWT middleware with ioredis sliding session store (TTL 3600s) because stateless tokens could not be revoked during the May 2 rate-limit incident.

sources.title: Webhook Reliability Design
sources.author: @alex_dev
sources.rawContent: Failed Stripe webhooks are retried synchronously up to 3 times via exponential backoff in the API route. This keeps ordering simple but adds latency to the webhook endpoint. Stripe requires acknowledgment within 10 seconds, so the third retry typically happens before a response is returned. If all retries fail we drop the event; a dead-letter queue was being evaluated for Q2.

facts.title: Webhook retries are synchronous in the API route
facts.summary: Failed Stripe webhooks are retried synchronously up to 3 times with exponential backoff inside the API route.
facts.verbatimQuote: Failed Stripe webhooks are retried synchronously up to 3 times via exponential backoff in the API route.

sources.title: feat: async webhook retries via SQS DLQ
sources.author: @sparsh_s
sources.rawContent: Moved failed Stripe webhooks to asynchronous AWS SQS dead-letter queue (payments-dlq.fifo). This branch replaces the synchronous retry path and keeps ordering guarantees via the FIFO queue. Needs one more approval before merge.

facts.title: Webhook retries move to async SQS DLQ
facts.summary: Failed Stripe webhooks move to an async SQS dead-letter queue (payments-dlq.fifo), replacing synchronous retries.
facts.verbatimQuote: Moved failed Stripe webhooks to asynchronous AWS SQS dead-letter queue (payments-dlq.fifo).

sources.title: Core Payments Service — System Architecture
sources.author: @alex_dev
sources.rawContent: Core Payments Service runs on AWS ECS Fargate behind an ALB. Deployment uses one ECS service per module with rolling deployments on Tuesdays. Secrets live in AWS Secrets Manager and are injected at task start. For anything infrastructure-related, talk to @ujjwal_t.

facts.title: Who to ask about deployment and infra
facts.summary: @ujjwal_t owns ECS, networks, and all infrastructure changes for Core Payments.
